summary: Likely synthetic: the AI-voice detector found synthetic-voice traces.

tests.name: AI Voice Detector
tests.explain: A wav2vec2 network, pre-trained on 960 hours of audiobook speech (LibriSpeech) and fine-tuned by its author on the In-the-Wild deepfake dataset, turns each 4-second window into 768 numbers describing its fine acoustic texture; a small logistic-regression 'probe' trained on our calibration clips reads them. It works best on voice generators like those it was tuned on - brand-new cloning tools can fool it.

tests.name: Spectral Cut-off
tests.finding: Recorded at 16 kHz - too low to see above 8 kHz.
tests.explain: Microphones record up to about 20 kHz, but many voice generators work at 16-24 kHz sample rates, so above 8-12 kHz their output can be an empty 'brick wall'. The chart shows where the long-term spectrum falls off. Phone calls, codecs and cheap mics cut off too, so in our experiment it did not separate real from fake: it is shown as evidence for your eyes, not scored.

tests.name: Prosody & Pitch
tests.finding: Pitch spread 3.4 semitones around 91 Hz; shown, not scored.
tests.explain: Pitch (F0) is how fast the vocal folds vibrate. We track it every 20 ms with the pYIN algorithm and plot its range and smoothness: flat, robotic intonation gave away older text-to-speech. Modern voice generators copy natural intonation, so in our experiment pitch did not separate real from fake; it is shown, not scored.

tests.name: Breaths & Silence
tests.finding: Very clean pauses (floor -97 dB); few or no breaths detected.
tests.explain: Unprocessed microphone recordings rarely contain true digital silence: between words there is room noise, and speakers take audible breaths. Many synthetic voices stitch words together over perfect zeros or a suspiciously clean noise floor, with no breaths. But call and voice-note apps often gate pauses to silence, so this is weak evidence (AUC 0.53 in our test). We map energy every 20 ms to find pauses, breaths and the noise floor.

tests.name: Spectrogram
tests.finding: Visual map of frequencies over time (not scored).
tests.explain: A spectrogram shows which frequencies are present at each moment: time runs left to right, pitch bottom to top (on the mel scale, which stretches low frequencies like our ears do), brightness is loudness. Harmonics appear as stacked bands, consonants as bursts of noise. It is a picture, not a score.
